title: Training for Aesthetics: You're doing it WRONG.
summary: Programming is only half the job; execution is the other half. He covers three things. Tempo: pick one controlled negative speed and keep it on every rep, warm-ups included, to justify the load, not to chase time under tension. Form: it must be repeatable and controlled, and a set ends when form breaks. Load: heavier only helps if the lift, technique and tempo are right.
claims: Programming is about 50% of results; executing it properly is the other 50%
Time under tension is a byproduct of slow tempo, like the pump is of high reps; chasing it makes you sacrifice load
Never sacrifice load for time under tension; priority order is load, then range of motion, then tempo
People overload by weight, volume or frequency because tempo is too hard to track
Slow tempo's real purpose is to keep ego in check so the load and range of motion are appropriate
Pick one tempo you like and stick to it regardless of load; any sensible tempo works
Do warm-ups at the same tempo as top sets; the advice to warm up fast is nonsense
Only control the negative; the positive is used as the fatigue gauge and you fail on it
Slow down most in the part of the range closest to the stretch; letting the bar drop there is cheating and where injuries happen
On the last rep near failure he lengthens the negative instead of rushing it
Good bodybuilding form means every rep is replicable and the lifter controls the weight
In bodybuilding form breakdown should never occur: when technique fails the set is over
When hips shoot up on squats, the stimulus shifts from quads to glutes and lower back; rack the bar at that point
Technical failure blocks muscular failure, which is why hack squats can beat high-bar squats for quads
Consistency, not stability, is the goal: unstable lifts like ring push-ups are fine if executed consistently
You should be able to justify every lift, rep range and frequency in your program
Thinking more weight always means faster growth is the number one mistake
Low-bar squats move more weight by biasing glutes and lower back; high-bar or hack squats move less weight but grow quads better
Load progression only matters if the lift is a good one and technique and tempo are controlled
He mocks an Instagram post claiming sloppy 3-plate barbell rows build more than strict 185 lb rows
Heavy weights can be lifted under control; intention is everything, you train to look better
exercises: removes technical failure, reach muscular failure
more load but biases glutes/lower back
